summary: Extends the BGP Graceful Restart mechanism to reduce the harm caused to MPLS forwarding when a Label Switching Router restarts. Traffic can keep flowing while the router recovers.

eli5.summary: When a router reboots, traffic usually gets dropped. This lets neighbors keep sending along the old routes for a short while, so the reboot is hardly noticed by MPLS users.

subtitle: How a router restarting its BGP can keep MPLS labels stable so traffic keeps flowing.

tldr.problem: When the BGP part of a Label Switching Router's control plane restarts, the MPLS label paths going through it may be disturbed even though its forwarding state could have been preserved.
tldr.mechanism: It extends BGP Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) so the restarting router either rebuilds the same label bindings it had before, or makes new ones while keeping the old forwarding state for a while, and neighbors treat labels like routes.
tldr.outcome: LSPs established by BGP need not be perturbed by a BGP restart, provided the router can preserve its MPLS forwarding state.

facts.label: Restarting LSR procedures
facts.value: Reconstruct the same bindings, or create new ones

facts.label: Spare labels needed (new-label approach)
facts.value: At least as many unallocated as allocated

facts.label: Label reuse hold-off
facts.value: At least the neighbor's Restart Time

today: RFC 4781 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on RFC 4724 for the base BGP Graceful Restart mechanism.

sections.title: The Problem and Scope
sections.content:
If a Label Switching Router (LSR) can preserve its MPLS forwarding state across a restart of its control plane, and BGP is used to carry MPLS labels (as in RFC 3107), it may be desirable not to perturb the LSPs going through that LSR after a failure or restart of its BGP component.

This mechanism works together with RFC 4724 and places no restrictions on address families. It applies to all LSRs. Those that cannot preserve forwarding state need only implement a subset (everything except the procedures in Sections 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 5), and their neighbors still benefit if the neighbors can preserve state.

By MPLS forwarding state the RFC means mappings such as incoming label -> (outgoing label, next hop) and FEC -> (outgoing label, next hop), plus the label-pop variants.
sections.eli5: When one router restarts its routing program, the roads through it should stay open. This RFC explains how to keep them open.

sections.title: General Requirements and Capability
sections.content:
An LSR MUST implement BGP Graceful Restart as in RFC 4724. It SHOULD be able to preserve its MPLS forwarding state across the restart. For FEC -> label bindings distributed via BGP, it SHOULD either reconstruct the same bindings (Section 4) or create new ones while temporarily keeping state for both old and new (Section 5).

While the LSR keeps preserved state, labels from that state cannot be used for new local bindings, though they can be used to reconstruct existing ones. For each next hop reachable via an LSP, the restarting LSR MUST be able to preserve the state of that LSP. If other protocols such as LDP or RSVP-TE also assign labels, the LSR MUST preserve which protocol assigned which label.

Support is advertised with the Graceful Restart Capability from RFC 4724. The SAFI in it MUST indicate that the NLRI carries labels as well as addresses. If the LSR can preserve its MPLS state, it SHOULD say so by setting the Flag for Address Family field for all applicable AFI/SAFI pairs.
sections.eli5: A router has to keep its old road map on the shelf, remember which helper handed out which road signs, and tell its neighbors that it has done so.

sections.title: Rebuilding the Same Labels
sections.content:
This approach applies when the restarting LSR can reconstruct the same FEC -> label bindings as before. After route selection per RFC 4724, one of three cases applies. The procedures are conceptual; only the externally visible behavior must match.

  • Case 1: the best route was received with a non-Implicit NULL label and the LSR advertises it with itself as next hop. The LSR looks in its preserved state for an entry matching the received outgoing label, next hop. If found, the entry is no longer stale and its incoming label is reused when advertising the route. Otherwise a new label is allocated.
  • Case 2: the route was received without a label, with Implicit NULL, or originated by the LSR, and the LSR must generate a non-Implicit NULL label. It looks for a label-pop entry with the same next hop and reuses its incoming label, or allocates a new one. If it uses a unique label per route, the FEC must also match.
  • Case 3: the LSR does not set the BGP next hop to self. It just uses the label received with the route, or no label if none was received, and allocates nothing.
sections.eli5: The router looks through its saved notes. If it finds the sign it used before for a road, it puts the same sign back up. If not, it makes a new one.

sections.title: Making New Labels While Keeping Old Ones
sections.content:
The alternative applies when the LSR does not reconstruct the same bindings but creates new ones after the restart, while temporarily maintaining forwarding state for both old and new. For this the LSR SHOULD have at least as many unallocated labels as it has labels allocated for BGP-distributed bindings. New bindings use unallocated labels as in the normal procedure.

The LSR SHOULD keep the preserved state at least until it sends an End-of-RIB marker to all its neighbors. It MAY keep it a bit longer, with the extra time possibly set by configuration, so neighbors can process its routes. Then it SHOULD delete the preserved state.

During this period a BGP route may have two local label bindings, one retained from before and one created after, but both have the same outgoing label and next hop.
sections.eli5: The router puts up brand-new signs while leaving the old ones standing for a while. Once all the neighbors have seen the new ones, the old signs come down.

sections.title: What Neighbors Do
sections.content:
A neighbor of a restarting LSR follows RFC 4724 and treats MPLS labels received from the restarting LSR the same way it treats routes. Replacing stale routes with new updates also means replacing or updating the labels. If the restarting LSR's capability flags show it could not retain MPLS state, the neighbor SHOULD immediately remove all NLRI and associated labels it learned from that LSR.

An LSR SHOULD keep the label in a label, FEC binding as long as it has a route to the FEC. When creating a new binding it SHOULD pick the least recently used label. After releasing a label, it SHALL NOT reuse it for a binding advertised to a graceful-restart-capable neighbor for at least the Restart Time that neighbor advertised. This applies to any label release at any time.
sections.eli5: Neighbors keep using the old signs for a short time. If the restarting router says it could not keep its notes, they throw the old signs away right away. Nobody reuses a retired sign too soon, so cars are not sent the wrong way.

sections.title: Comparing the Two Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC compares the two restart procedures directly.

  • The same-label procedures (Section 4) involve more computational overhead on the restarting router than the new-label procedures (Section 5).
  • The new-label procedures need twice as many labels.
  • The same-label procedures cause fewer changes to MPLS forwarding state in the neighbors.

In principle an LSR may use the first approach for some AFI/SAFIs and the second for others.
sections.eli5: Reusing old signs takes more thinking by the router but is gentler on its neighbors. Making new signs needs twice as many signs but less thinking.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of BGP (RFC 4271) remain relevant. The mechanism also exposes LSRs to extra denial-of-service attacks. An intruder could impersonate a BGP peer to force the TCP connection to fail and reconnect with the Forwarding State (F) bit set to 0, or intercept traffic and override the F bit to 0. Either forces all labels received from that peer to be released. Authentication between BGP peers, such as RFC 2385, counters these attacks.

There is also the risk of using a label after the BGP session that created it has expired, which could misroute data. Since the session may be extended by the Restart Time, and a downstream LSR may declare failure earlier, the RFC requires that labels are not reused until at least the Restart Time has passed.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could trick a router into thinking its neighbor lost its notes, so it throws away good signs. Checking who is really talking, and not reusing signs too quickly, protects against that.
